title: Snib and the Sparrow Secret
markdown:
Once upon a time, high in the Whispering Peaks, where gardens clung to mountainsides like colourful patches on a giant quilt and lakes sparkled like spilled jewels, lived a rather special goblin named Snib. While others would flap their arms and declare the sky about to somersault, or that a grumpy badger had stolen the sun, Snib preferred a quieter investigation. He’d wiggle his fingers, prod a bit, adjust a screw, and usually find a perfectly sensible answer. His most constant companion was Maple, a badger pup, whirlwind of soft fur and boundless curiosity. Her happy yips and worried whimpers mattered more to him than any grand pronouncement from the elders.

Every day was a delightful puzzle. If a watering pipe on the tippy-top terrace sprang a leak, other goblins rushed about imagining the mountain turning into a mudslide. Snib fetched vine, a generous clump of moss, and a smooth well-chosen stone. A few clever twists, and the leak was sealed. Maple’s tail blurred, as if to say well done.

Until one day the valley was jolted by something truly strange. The bells — the big booming ones that told everyone breakfast time or important news — began to ring in the most frightful topsy-turvy way. Dong-clang-whoosh from the biggest, goblins leaping back, furry hands to ears. Then a hasty tinkle-tinkle-thump, a long wobbly bong-silence. The air felt cold. Even the bravest whiskers quivered.

The village elders, important-looking goblins with beards that tickled their knees, declared it a sign of bad luck. They whispered of the sky tumbling in chunks, of ancient dragons rudely woken. Alarming declarations filled the terraced gardens. Snib watched Maple’s usually cheerful ears droop and felt a different prickle. Chaotic, yes. But a pattern. A mechanical pattern. His curious eyes scanned the distant bell tower.

“Come along, Maple. Let’s go see why those bells are being so dreadfully impolite.”

Because of that choice they followed narrow paths that clung to sheer sides like tiny brave lizards, past ancient firs that seemed to sigh secrets, through meadows of hardy colourful flowers. A soft silvery mist drifted through firs below a crumbling old tower.

Their path led to the Great Stone Bridge, flung across a deep echoing gorge as if by a giant’s playful hand. Guarding it, as always, was Grunk the ogre: immense, skin like mossy rocks, voice a tiny distant avalanche. “Halt. No one crosses without my say-so. And those bells. They’re making my ears ache something awful.”

Snib stood as tall as he could. “A good day to you, Grunk. We’re not here to cause bother. We just want to understand why the bells are making such a peculiar clatter-clatter-jangle.” With a flourish he offered a small perfectly ripe mountain berry from his pouch.

Grunk eyed the bright red berry, then Snib. “Clatter-clatter-jangle is putting it mildly. It’s an outrage. But you do speak a sensible truth. What do you think should be done?”

“Likely just a bit of dust, or a tiny cog slipped. I can build a simple contraption to clean it out.”

Grunk, terribly tired of the clanging, grunted. “Fine. But if you make it worse, you’re both going to be mending it with your own noisy hands.”

Until finally, after winding stairs and a great deal of fiddling with pulleys, brushes, and enormous feather dusters that tickled Maple’s nose, Snib discovered the truth. A family of particularly bold mountain sparrows had decided the bell tower was the most perfect place in the world for a very large messy nest. Comings and goings, loose twigs, stray feathers: the ancient mechanism gone higgledy-piggledy. He held his breath. A soft whirr from the gears, then stillness. A clear bright bong vibrated through the stone. The air, once thick with dust and feathers, tasted clean. As a peace offering he fashioned a charming miniature birdhouse and hung it nearby. Maple wagged with delight. The valley’s bells, free of their fluttery overlords, rang clear and harmonious.

Ever since then, when a pipe leaked or a bell wobbled, the elders still made their pronouncements — but they often began, “Now, as Snib might suggest.” And Maple’s yip, at the first true bong, was the only speech the mountain really needed.
characters: Snib (a goblin), Maple (a badger pup), Grunk (an ogre bridge-keeper)
audience: children aged 11-12, amusing mountain fantasy adventure for older children
author: StoryGen Community
